newsitem.title: GERMANY: German farmers angry over EU reform plans-leader.
newsitem.headline: German farmers angry over EU reform plans-leader.

text.p: German farmers are angry at the prospect of income losses from a European Commission plan to cut prices ahead of future world trade talks and EU eastward expansion, said farm union (DBV) president Gerd Sonnleitner.

In an interview with Reuters at the union's headquarters he said, "Farmers are very nervous -- they see that their incomes are lagging behind those of other groups in society, and now they are asked to accept even more losses."
"I find this a highly explosive situation."
Sonnleitner said details of the price-cutting proposals, tabled by the EU Commission on Wednesday, were only emerging bit by bit, but DBV was surprised by their radical nature.
DBV, which represents 90 percent of Germany's 550,000 farms, estimates its members could lose one fifth of their incomes, should the plans go ahead.
The plans envisage cutting cereals, beef and dairy prices by 20, 30, and 10 percent respectively by 2006, while accompanying rises in direct aid will not fully offset them.
DBV was disappointed there had been no consultations and exchanges of ideas before the plan was presented.
The proposals could bring savings of 3.7 billion Ecus in intervention and export refunds by 2006, according to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
But higher compensation payments might add 7.7 billion Ecus, including 4.1 billion for beef producers, by that date.
Sonnleitner said a public increasingly hostile to the farmers' cause might interpret the reform as another budgetary burden -- adding insult to injury in his opinion.
Oilseed producers, for example, could lose a third of their current returns per hectare from the new non-crop specific area aid as yield increases could not offset such a sharp cut.

DBV, together with its European partner organisations, believed farmers had made enough sacrifices under 1992 farm reform when grain prices had been cut, protection from exports lowered, and when the oilseeds area was permanently limited.
"There should not be any premature concessions ahead of new world trade talks," Sonnleitner said.
Elsewhere, DBV was furious at learning maize for silage would be excluded from the grain regime, which would hurt dairy farmers. -Vera Eckert, Bonn newsroom, +49-228-26097145
